dryRun.title: readFile("a", cb) — the Node callback convention
rows: readFile starts the work and returns at once
callback inside callback inside callback… (callback hell)
dryRun.note: A callback is a function you hand over to be called later. Node style is error-first: cb(err, result). Nesting many dependent steps creates "callback hell": deep indentation and error handling repeated at every level. Promises fix this.

think.q:
function later(cb) { setTimeout(() => cb(null, 'done'), 0) }
later((err, v) => console.log(v))
console.log('first')
why: later returns immediately; the callback runs after the current code has finished.

think.q:
function bad(cb) { if (Math.random() < 2) return cb('sync'); setTimeout(() => cb('async')) }
bad((v) => console.log(v))
console.log('after')
why: This function sometimes calls back synchronously and sometimes later ("releasing Zalgo"). Callers cannot predict the order. Always call back asynchronously, or always synchronously.

think.q:
let calls = 0
function once(cb) { cb(); cb() }
once(() => calls++)
console.log(calls)
why: Nothing stops a buggy API from calling your callback twice. Promises guarantee settle-once.
think.exec:
let calls = 0
function once(cb) { cb(); cb() }
once(() => calls++)
console.log(calls)

think.q:
function step(n, cb) { setTimeout(() => cb(null, n + 1), 0) }
step(1, (e, a) => step(a, (e, b) => step(b, (e, c) => console.log(c))))
why: Three dependent steps already nest three levels deep. That pyramid is callback hell.
think.exec:
function step(n, cb) { setTimeout(() => cb(null, n + 1), 0) }
step(1, (e, a) => step(a, (e, b) => step(b, (e, c) => console.log(c))))

think.q: In fs.readFile(path, (err, data) => …), what must the callback do first?
opts: Check err and return early if it is set
why: Error-first callbacks put the failure first so it cannot be forgotten.

try.task: Write promisify(fn): turn an error-first callback function into one that returns a Promise (resolve with result, reject with err).
examples: const wait = promisify((ms, cb) => setTimeout(() => cb(null, ms), ms)); await wait(5)  // 5
try.hint: Return (...args) => new Promise((res, rej) => fn(...args, (err, val) => err ? rej(err) : res(val))).

checks.verify: const wait = promisify((ms, cb) => setTimeout(() => cb(null, ms), ms)); assert((await wait(5)) === 5, "resolve")
let e; try { await promisify((cb) => cb(new Error("x")))() } catch (x) { e = x }; assert(e && e.message === "x", "reject")
const add = promisify((a, b, cb) => cb(null, a + b)); assert((await add(2, 3)) === 5, "args")

takeaway.key: A callback runs later; Node uses cb(err, result). Callbacks nest, repeat error handling and can be called twice: promises solve all three.
mistakes: Ignoring err in an error-first callback.
APIs that call back sometimes sync, sometimes async.

dryRun.title: console.log("A"); setTimeout(() => console.log("B")); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("C")); console.log("D")
dryRun.note: JavaScript runs one thing at a time. When the stack is empty, the event loop first runs all microtasks (promise callbacks), then one macrotask (timer, I/O, event), then microtasks again, and so on. Output: A D C B.

think.q:
console.log('A')
setTimeout(() => console.log('B'))
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('C'))
console.log('D')
why: Sync code first (A, D), then microtasks (C), then the timer (B).
think.exec:
console.log('A')
setTimeout(() => console.log('B'))
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('C'))
console.log('D')

think.q:
setTimeout(() => console.log('t1'), 0)
setTimeout(() => console.log('t2'), 0)
Promise.resolve().then(() => { console.log('p1'); setTimeout(() => console.log('t3')) })
why: p1 is a microtask, so it runs first. t3 is queued after t1 and t2.
think.exec:
setTimeout(() => console.log('t1'), 0)
setTimeout(() => console.log('t2'), 0)
Promise.resolve().then(() => { console.log('p1'); setTimeout(() => console.log('t3')) })

think.q:
const start = Date.now()
setTimeout(() => console.log(Date.now() - start >= 50), 0)
while (Date.now() - start < 50) {}
why: A 0 ms timer still waits for the stack to be empty. The busy loop blocks for 50 ms, so the timer fires late.

think.q:
let n = 0
Promise.resolve().then(() => n++)
console.log(n)
queueMicrotask(() => console.log(n))
why: then callbacks never run synchronously. By the time the queued microtask logs, the earlier then has run.
think.exec:
let n = 0
Promise.resolve().then(() => n++)
console.log(n)
queueMicrotask(() => console.log(n))

think.q: Why does a long synchronous loop freeze the page (no clicks, no painting)?
opts: The browser limits loops to 1 second
The event loop cannot run anything else until the stack is empty
why: Rendering and events are tasks too. Split long work into chunks or move it to a worker.

try.task: Write order() that returns a Promise resolving to the array of labels in the order they actually ran, for: sync "s1", setTimeout "t", Promise.then "p", queueMicrotask "m", sync "s2". Then check it matches ["s1", "s2", "p", "m", "t"].
examples: (microtasks run in the order they were queued)
try.hint: Push each label into an array from where it runs; resolve the array inside a second setTimeout so everything else has finished.

checks.verify: assert(order() instanceof Promise, "promise")
const r = await order(); assert(r[0] === "s1" && r[1] === "s2", "sync first")
const r = await order(); assert(r.join() === "s1,s2,p,m,t", r.join())

takeaway.key: Stack first, then ALL microtasks, then ONE macrotask, repeat. A 0 ms timer runs after promises and after any blocking code.
mistakes: Expecting setTimeout(fn, 0) to run before promise callbacks.
Blocking the main thread with long loops.

dryRun.title: Which queue?
rows: right after current code, before anything else
dryRun.note: Microtasks are drained completely, even ones added while draining. So a microtask that keeps queueing microtasks starves timers and rendering forever.

think.q:
setTimeout(() => console.log('timeout'))
Promise.resolve().then(() => { console.log('m1'); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('m2')) })
why: The microtask queue is drained fully, including m2 added during m1, before the timer.
think.exec:
setTimeout(() => console.log('timeout'))
Promise.resolve().then(() => { console.log('m1'); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('m2')) })

think.q:
(async () => { console.log('a'); await null; console.log('b') })()
console.log('c')
why: An async function runs synchronously until its first await; the rest is a microtask.
think.exec:
(async () => { console.log('a'); await null; console.log('b') })()
console.log('c')

think.q:
const p = new Promise((res) => { console.log('executor'); res(1) })
p.then(() => console.log('then'))
console.log('sync')
why: The Promise executor runs synchronously. Only then callbacks are deferred.

think.q:
let i = 0
function loop() { if (++i < 1000) queueMicrotask(loop) }
loop()
setTimeout(() => console.log('timer', i))
why: All 999 queued microtasks finish before the timer gets a turn. With no limit, this would block forever.
think.exec:
let i = 0
function loop() { if (++i < 1000) queueMicrotask(loop) }
loop()
setTimeout(() => console.log('timer', i))

think.q: Why does it matter in UI code that promise callbacks run before the next paint?
opts: Promises always run in a worker
State updates in a promise chain are applied together before the browser paints, so you see no half-updated screen
why: Long microtask chains also delay that paint, which makes the UI feel stuck.

try.task: Write nextTick() (resolves in a microtask), nextMacrotask() (resolves in a timer), and race2() that starts both and returns a Promise of which one finished first ("micro" or "macro").
try.hint: nextTick = () => Promise.resolve(); nextMacrotask = () => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r)); then Promise.race with labels.

checks.verify: assert(nextTick() instanceof Promise && nextMacrotask() instanceof Promise, "promises")
assert((await race2()) === "micro", "order")
const log = []; const p = nextMacrotask().then(() => log.push("macro")); nextTick().then(() => log.push("micro")); await p; assert(log.join() === "micro,macro", log.join())

takeaway.key: Microtasks (promises, await, queueMicrotask) run before the next macrotask (timers, events) and are drained completely.
mistakes: Endless microtask chains that starve rendering and timers.
Thinking a Promise executor runs asynchronously.

dryRun.title: fetchUser().then(getPosts).then(render).catch(show)
dryRun.note: A Promise is a placeholder for a future value: pending → fulfilled or rejected, exactly once. then returns a new promise, so you chain instead of nesting. Returning a promise from then makes the chain wait for it.

think.q: Promise.resolve(1).then((x) => x + 1).then((x) => { throw new Error('e' + x) }).catch((e) => e.message).then(console.log)
why: 1 → 2 → throws "e2" → catch turns it back into a value "e2" → logged.
think.exec: Promise.resolve(1).then((x) => x + 1).then((x) => { throw new Error('e' + x) }).catch((e) => e.message).then(console.log)

think.q:
const p = new Promise((res, rej) => { res('first'); rej('second'); res('third') })
p.then(console.log, console.log)
why: A promise settles once. Later resolve/reject calls are ignored.
think.exec:
const p = new Promise((res, rej) => { res('first'); rej('second'); res('third') })
p.then(console.log, console.log)

think.q: Promise.resolve(1).then(2).then((x) => console.log(x))
why: then ignores non-function arguments and passes the value through.
think.exec: Promise.resolve(1).then(2).then((x) => console.log(x))

think.q:
const p = Promise.resolve(5)
console.log(p === Promise.resolve(p), typeof p.then)
why: Promise.resolve returns the same promise if you give it one. A thenable is anything with a then method.
think.exec:
const p = Promise.resolve(5)
console.log(p === Promise.resolve(p), typeof p.then)

think.q: getUser().then((u) => { getPosts(u) }).then((posts) => render(posts)) — render gets undefined. Why?
opts: The first callback does not return getPosts(u), so the chain does not wait for it
why: Inside { } you must write return. Forgetting it is the most common promise bug.

try.task: Implement delay(ms) and withTimeout(promise, ms): the second resolves like the given promise, but rejects with Error("timeout") if it takes longer than ms.
try.hint: delay: new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, ms)). withTimeout: Promise.race with a promise that rejects after ms.

checks.verify: const t0 = Date.now(); await delay(20); assert(Date.now() - t0 >= 15, "sleep")
assert((await withTimeout(sleep(5).then(() => "ok"), 100)) === "ok", "fast")
let e; try { await withTimeout(sleep(100), 10) } catch (x) { e = x }; assert(e && e.message === "timeout", "timeout")

takeaway.key: A promise settles once. then returns a new promise; return values (or promises) flow down the chain; one catch handles any earlier failure.
mistakes: Forgetting return inside a then callback.
Expecting resolve after resolve to change anything.

dryRun.title: async function load() { const u = await getUser(); const p = await getPosts(u); return p.length }
rows: runs until the first await, returns a pending promise
load resumes (as a microtask), u is set
the promise from load() fulfills with it
dryRun.note: async functions always return a promise. await pauses only that function until the promise settles, then gives the value or throws the rejection, so normal try/catch works.

think.q:
async function f() { return 1 }
console.log(f() instanceof Promise, typeof f())
why: An async function always returns a promise, even for a plain return value.
think.exec:
async function f() { return 1 }
console.log(f() instanceof Promise, typeof f())

think.q:
const wait = (ms, v) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(() => r(v), ms))
async function seq() { const t = Date.now(); await wait(30); await wait(30); return Date.now() - t >= 55 }
async function par() { const t = Date.now(); await Promise.all([wait(30), wait(30)]); return Date.now() - t < 55 }
Promise.all([seq(), par()]).then((r) => console.log(r.join(' ')))
why: Two awaits in a row wait one after the other (~60 ms). Promise.all runs them at the same time (~30 ms).

think.q:
async function f() { try { await Promise.reject(new Error('no')) } catch (e) { return 'caught ' + e.message } }
f().then(console.log)
why: await turns a rejection into a throw, so try/catch handles it.
think.exec:
async function f() { try { await Promise.reject(new Error('no')) } catch (e) { return 'caught ' + e.message } }
f().then(console.log)

think.q:
const results = []
;[3, 1, 2].forEach(async (n) => { await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, n)); results.push(n) })
console.log(results.length)
why: forEach does not wait for async callbacks; when we log, none has finished. Use for…of with await, or Promise.all with map.
think.exec:
const results = []
;[3, 1, 2].forEach(async (n) => { await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, n)); results.push(n) })
console.log(results.length)

think.q: How do you use await outside an async function?
opts: In an ES module (top-level await), or by wrapping code in an async IIFE
why: Classic scripts need an async function around the await.

try.task: Write mapLimit(items, limit, fn): run async fn(item) for every item with at most limit running at once, and resolve to the results in the original order.
examples: // never more than 2 calls in flight
try.hint: Start limit workers; each worker loops: take the next index, await fn, store the result at that index.

checks.verify: const r = await mapLimit([30, 5, 15], 2, (ms) => sleep(ms).then(() => ms)); assert(JSON.stringify(r) === "[30,5,15]", JSON.stringify(r))

checks.t: never more than limit at once
checks.verify: let now = 0, max = 0; await mapLimit([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], 2, async () => { now++; max = Math.max(max, now); await sleep(5); now-- }); assert(max === 2, "max in flight " + max)

checks.t: empty input resolves to an empty array
checks.verify: const r = await mapLimit([], 3, async (x) => x); assert(Array.isArray(r) && r.length === 0, "empty")

takeaway.key: async returns a promise; await pauses the function and throws on rejection. Sequential awaits are slow when the work is independent: use Promise.all.
mistakes: Forgetting that an async function returns a promise, not the value.

dryRun.title: Three requests: A ok (30 ms), B fails (10 ms), C ok (20 ms)
dryRun.note: all: everything must succeed. allSettled: wait for all, never rejects. race: first to settle, success or failure. any: first success; rejects with AggregateError only if all fail.

think.q:
const ok = (v, ms) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(() => r(v), ms))
const no = (e, ms) => new Promise((_, j) => setTimeout(() => j(e), ms))
Promise.all([ok('A', 30), no('B', 10), ok('C', 20)]).then(console.log, (e) => console.log('rejected', e))
why: all rejects as soon as one input rejects.

think.q:
const ok = (v, ms) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(() => r(v), ms))
const no = (e, ms) => new Promise((_, j) => setTimeout(() => j(e), ms))
Promise.allSettled([ok('A', 30), no('B', 10)]).then((r) => console.log(r.map((x) => x.status).join()))
why: allSettled reports every result, in input order.

think.q:
const ok = (v, ms) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(() => r(v), ms))
const no = (e, ms) => new Promise((_, j) => setTimeout(() => j(e), ms))
Promise.any([no('B', 10), ok('C', 20), ok('A', 30)]).then(console.log)
why: any ignores failures and takes the first success.

think.q: Promise.any([Promise.reject(1), Promise.reject(2)]).catch((e) => console.log(e.constructor.name, e.errors.join()))
why: When all fail, any rejects with an AggregateError holding every reason, in input order.
think.exec: Promise.any([Promise.reject(1), Promise.reject(2)]).catch((e) => console.log(e.constructor.name, e.errors.join()))

think.q: You load a dashboard from 5 widgets; one broken widget must not hide the other four. Which?
why: allSettled lets you render what succeeded and show an error for the rest.

try.task: Implement promiseAll(promises) without using Promise.all: resolve to the values in input order, reject on the first rejection, and resolve to [] for an empty array. Plain (non-promise) values are allowed.
try.hint: Count how many have resolved; store each value at its index; wrap each item with Promise.resolve.

checks.t: keeps input order, not finish order
checks.verify: const r = await promiseAll([sleep(20).then(() => "a"), "b", sleep(5).then(() => "c")]); assert(JSON.stringify(r) === '["a","b","c"]', JSON.stringify(r))
let e; try { await promiseAll([sleep(30), Promise.reject(new Error("x"))]) } catch (x) { e = x }; assert(e && e.message === "x", "reject")
const r = await promiseAll([]); assert(Array.isArray(r) && r.length === 0, "empty")

takeaway.key: all = all must succeed, allSettled = report everything, race = first settled, any = first success.
mistakes: Using all when one failure should not hide the rest.
Expecting race to ignore failures (that is any).

dryRun.title: Where does a rejection go?
dryRun.note: Every promise chain needs an end: an await inside try/catch, or a final .catch. A rejection nobody handles fires unhandledrejection in browsers and crashes modern Node.

think.q:
async function f() { throw new Error('x') }
let p
try { p = f(); console.log('no sync throw') } catch { console.log('caught sync') }
p.catch((e) => console.log('caught async', e.message))
why: f() returns a rejected promise; nothing is thrown synchronously, so the try/catch sees nothing. Only .catch (or await) handles it.

think.q: Promise.reject(new Error('a')).then(() => console.log('ok'), (e) => console.log('handled', e.message)).then(() => console.log('continues'))
why: The second then argument handles the rejection, and the chain continues fulfilled.
think.exec: Promise.reject(new Error('a')).then(() => console.log('ok'), (e) => console.log('handled', e.message)).then(() => console.log('continues'))

think.q: Promise.resolve().then(() => { throw new Error('in ok') }, () => console.log('never')).catch((e) => console.log('later catch', e.message))
why: The second argument of a then only handles the promise before it, not errors thrown by its own first argument. A trailing catch does.
think.exec: Promise.resolve().then(() => { throw new Error('in ok') }, () => console.log('never')).catch((e) => console.log('later catch', e.message))

think.q:
async function a() { await Promise.reject(new Error('deep')) }
async function b() { try { await a() } catch (e) { return 'b handled ' + e.message } }
b().then(console.log)
why: Awaited rejections travel up through async functions like thrown errors.

think.q: saveDraft() is async and you call it without await in an event handler. What should you add?
why: A fire-and-forget promise needs its own .catch, or its failure is unhandled.

try.task: Write retry(fn, times, delayMs): call async fn; if it rejects, wait delayMs and try again, up to times attempts in total. Resolve with the first success; if all fail, reject with the last error.
examples: await retry(flaky, 3, 5)  // succeeds on the 3rd try
await retry(alwaysFails, 2, 5)  // rejects with the 2nd error
try.hint: A for loop with try/catch around await fn(); remember the last error; await sleep between attempts.

checks.verify: let n = 0; const r = await retry(async () => { if (++n < 3) throw new Error("f" + n); return "ok" }, 3, 1); assert(r === "ok" && n === 3, "retry")
let n = 0, e; try { await retry(async () => { throw new Error("f" + ++n) }, 2, 1) } catch (x) { e = x }; assert(e && e.message === "f2" && n === 2, "last error")
let n = 0; await retry(async () => ++n, 5, 1); assert(n === 1, "called " + n)

takeaway.key: Await inside try/catch or end every chain with .catch. try/catch around a non-awaited async call catches nothing.
mistakes: Calling an async function without await or .catch.
Using then(ok, bad) and expecting bad to catch errors thrown in ok.
